output.brief: The shortfall is mostly a pricing problem, not an Admissions Office failure. Applications, admit numbers and admit quality all rose. Yield fell only in the tiers where the Board cut awards: Dean's awards went from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield fell from 45% to 32%. Merit awards went from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield fell from 45% to 32%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield held at about 36%. The no-award group barely moved, from 38.5% to 37.0%. So this is not a general softening in demand. Early-action students got decisions on time, on the old system, yet their yield fell about as much as regular-decision yield (7.4 against 7.5 points). That makes the slow portal turnaround an unlikely main cause, though it was real and probably hurt some individual students. Missing-transcript claims are unverified. I'm fairly confident in this, but one gap remains: the data doesn't split tiers by round. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a costed proposal to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers before award letters go out. Separately, set a regular-decision turnaround target and restore merit-review staffing. Hold off on the portal rebuild until the document-loss claim is checked.
